---
title: "A Bioconductor MCP server: one public surface, ops first"
date: 2026-10-22
---

::: {.callout-note}
## Status: proposal, draft (2026-10-22)
A spec for Bioconductor's public MCP server. It revises the split in
[#67](https://github.com/seandavi/bioc-infrastructure/issues/67) ("split by audience"): servers
split by trust, and audiences become modules inside one server. The first modules serve the ops
and core-team audience. Nothing here is built. Measurements are from 2026-10-22.
:::

## Summary

One remote MCP server for Bioconductor, running on a Cloudflare Worker (Hono). v0 ships three
modules (`docs`, `pkg`, `ops`); later audiences add modules, not servers. It adds no new data
and no new API. Each tool is a thin adapter over an endpoint that already exists, and one tool
searches these docs so that someone asking "why does the stack work this way?" gets the ADR
instead of a guess.

v0 is read-only, unauthenticated and public. It serves only what is already public: the
registry, bioconductor.org, r-universe, public GitHub repos and this site. Anything that is not
already public (the `bioc-health` bundle, traffic beyond the published stats, reviews in
progress) is out of v0 by construction, so the server cannot leak anything.

## One public server, split by trust

There will be more than one Bioconductor MCP server, but only where a trust boundary forces it:

| Server | Runs | Trust | Contents |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Bioconductor MCP** (this spec) | Remote Worker | Public data only, no auth | Modules: `docs`, `pkg`, `ops` in v0; later `impact`, `contrib`, maintainer tools |
| **Operator MCP** | Remote, auth-gated | Non-public data | Only when a real question needs it; none does yet |
| **In-session R MCP** ({mcptools}, OS4LS WP2) | Local, in the user's R session | The user's machine | Live object introspection; cannot be remote |

Audiences are **modules**, not servers. Separate servers per audience would mean separate deploys,
separate URLs for users to configure, and eventually a gateway to put them back together. A
gateway earns its place when other teams run servers independently (the OLS MCP, or r-universe if
it ships one); for one team running one stack, a Worker with one module per domain already does
the gateway's job.

**Context cost, the real downside of one big server, is handled by toolset paths.** The same Worker
serves `/mcp` (every module) and `/mcp/{module}[+{module}…]` (a subset: `/mcp/ops`,
`/mcp/docs+pkg`). Tool names carry their module as a prefix (`docs_search`, `pkg_status`,
`ops_activity`), so the full set stays readable and never collides. A user who only wants docs
search pays for two tool descriptions, not twenty.

**Rule for adding a module:** its data is already public, and its tools follow the adapter and
provenance rules below. Anything failing the first test goes to the operator server.

## Why this order

- **API first, MCP as adapter.** Every tool maps to an endpoint a person can `curl`. When a tool
  answers wrongly, the cause is either the adapter or the API, and the API can be checked on its
  own.
- **Existing APIs first.** Building the server shows which questions the current APIs answer
  badly (see [Gaps it will expose](#gaps)). Those gaps become the case for the registry and
  health APIs, measured instead of guessed.
- **Docs search alongside.** Most questions from the core team are "why" or "how", not "what
  state is it in". ADRs 0001–0013, the runbooks and the plans already answer them, but only
  for someone who knows which page to open.

## Tools (v0)

Eight tools in three modules, each read-only. Descriptions are written for the model: what the tool answers, and
which tool to use instead when it doesn't fit.

| Tool | Answers | Backed by |
|---|---|---|
| `docs_search(query, limit=8)` | "Why/how does X work?": ranked sections with title, URL, breadcrumb and snippet | Docs index (below) |
| `docs_read(url)` | The full text of one page or section from `docs_search` | Same index |
| `pkg_status(package, universe="bioc")` | Is it propagated, at which version and commit; the upstream build's status, per-config check verdicts, BiocCheck verdict, and whether a newer commit failed | Registry `GET /data/prop/{universe}/index.json` (one entry) + r-universe `GET https://{universe}.r-universe.dev/api/packages/{pkg}` (`_status`, `_jobs`, `_bioccheck`, `_commit`, `_failure`) |
| `pkg_check_output(universe, job, file="00check.log")` | Why a check failed: the `ERROR`/`WARNING` sections of the check output, not the whole file | Registry `GET /checks/{universe}/{job}` |
| `pkg_build_environment(universe, job)` | What the build actually ran with: image digest, repos | Registry `GET /builds/{universe}/{job}` |
| `pkg_release_info()` | Current release and devel, associated R versions, published manifests | `bioconductor.org/config.yaml` + `GET /api/v1/manifest/index.json` |
| `pkg_downloads(package, year?)` | Monthly distinct clients and downloads under the published `/packages/stats` definition, with the data-as-of date | `bioconductor.org/packages/stats/bioc/{pkg}/{pkg}_{year}_stats.tab` |
| `ops_activity(repo?)` | Open issues and PRs, failing default-branch workflows, `<unit> is failing` issues from `bioc-notify@`, across the `seandavi/bioc-*` repos | GitHub REST, read-only |

### Resources

- `bioc://docs/{path}`: each docs page, so a client can attach `operations.html` or an ADR
  directly.
- `bioc://about`: what the server covers, what each source is, and the freshness of each.
  This is the answer to "can I trust this number?", written once.

### Prompts

- `triage-failing-package(package)`: `pkg_status` → `pkg_check_output` for the failing config →
  `docs_search` for the relevant gate or runbook.
- `explain-decision(topic)`: `docs_search` restricted to `adr/`, then `docs_read`, quoted with
  links.

### Out of v0, deliberately

- **SQL.** The registry's `/sql` console runs DuckDB-WASM in the browser, and DuckDB is too heavy
  for a Worker. For history questions, `pkg_status` returns a ready-to-run query and a link
  to `/sql`, and does not execute it.
- **`bioc-health` findings.** `bundle.json` exists only on onclappc02. Publishing it is v1 (see
  [Next](#next)).
- **Writes of any kind,** including re-running workflows, closing issues and purging caches.
  Those belong to the Factory layer in
  [#43](https://github.com/seandavi/bioc-infrastructure/issues/43), with its own permission
  model.
- **Bioconductor/Contributions review data.** It is public, so it can come later as a `contrib`
  module.

## Docs search

**Corpus.**

1. This site's Quarto `search.json`: 264 sections across 41 pages, ADRs included, with
   `href`, `title`, `section`, `crumbs` and `text` already split by heading. No crawler is needed.
2. The component repos' own docs, which are not on this site: `bioc-registry/docs/api.md`,
   `bioc-edge/DATAPLANE.md`, `bioc-traffic/docs/*.md`, and the READMEs of the `bioc-*` repos.
   These are split by heading into the same record shape, with a `repo` field and a GitHub URL.

**Index: lexical first.** The MCP repo's CI fetches the published records (this site's
`search.json` and the component docs, all public URLs), builds a BM25 index (MiniSearch,
serialized JSON) and deploys it with the Worker. It runs daily and on a `repository_dispatch`
sent by this site's docs deploy. The Worker loads the index once per isolate and caches it. The whole corpus is a few hundred sections, small enough to hold in memory.

This follows the cost ladder in the [unified-search proposal](proposal-unified-search.qmd):
static index first, managed semantic search (Cloudflare AI Search / Vectorize) only if tests
show a gain. The test is a fixed set of about 30 real questions (from issues, the
`bioc-health` skill and this conversation's history), each with the section that answers it.
If lexical recall@5 falls below about 80%, try embeddings and compare on the same set.

**Freshness.** The index is rebuilt on every docs deploy, so it is never staler than the site.
The `bioc://about` resource reports the index build time and commit.

## Architecture

```
MCP client ──POST /mcp[/module]──▶ bioc-mcp Worker (Hono)
                           ├─ modules: docs · pkg · ops (toolset chosen by path)
                           ├─ adapters: one per upstream
                           │    registry · r-universe · bioconductor.org · GitHub
                           ├─ docs index (JSON asset, built in CI)
                           └─ Cache API: per-upstream TTLs
```

- **Protocol:** MCP spec `2026-07-28`, Streamable HTTP. That revision is stateless (no
  sessions, no `initialize` handshake), which fits a Worker with no Durable Object. Use the
  official SDK's Hono adapter (`@modelcontextprotocol/hono`, `createMcpHandler`), and set
  `allowedHosts` to the deployed hostname.
- **Adapters are pure:** `fetch upstream → shape → return structuredContent + a short text
  summary`. Each declares an `outputSchema`. Tests run against recorded upstream fixtures, like
  `health/tests` pins rules against config.
- **Every result carries provenance:** the upstream URL(s) it came from and their freshness
  (`ts`, `DATA_AS_OF`, `generated`). An agent quoting a number can say where it came from.
- **Size discipline:** no tool returns more than about 8 KB of text. Check output is cut to its
  failing sections, and lists are paginated with a `cursor`.
- **Caching:** registry index 5 min, r-universe 5 min, stats 1 h, `config.yaml` and manifests
  1 h, GitHub 2 min. Results also carry the MCP `ttlMs` hint.
- **GitHub:** a fine-grained token with *no* repository permissions (public read only) as a
  Worker secret, for the 5,000/h rate limit. It cannot write.
- **Abuse:** Cloudflare rate limiting per IP on `/mcp`. Every tool call is logged as `{tool,
  args-shape, latency, upstream status}`, without arguments that could identify people. That
  log is the usage metric (and the U24 aim 4D metric).
- **Language: TypeScript.** Workers run it natively; the official SDK's Hono adapter targets the
  stateless `2026-07-28` protocol; and MiniSearch builds the docs index in CI and loads it in
  the Worker, so one library reads its own serialized format. Python (FastMCP) would need a
  host. The cost is contributors, who know R and Python first. A module is a few dozen lines
  (fetch, shape, zod schema) copied from a template, and eval questions and docs sources are
  YAML or Markdown. If a module needs real computation, a Python or R producer publishes JSON
  and the TypeScript adapter reads it.
- **Separate from the registry Worker.** MCP traffic never touches the install path (#67's
  "split producers").
- **Where it lives:** its own repo, `seandavi/bioc-mcp`, moving to the `Bioconductor` org when
  the core team adopts it (GitHub redirects the old URL). It is a named exception to ADR 0014's
  operated-stack monorepo and single tracker, on two grounds:
  - **It shares no code with the stack.** Every input, this site's `search.json` included, is a
    published artifact at a public URL, the same way it reads r-universe.
  - **Its contributors are not the stack's.** New modules, docs sources and eval questions are
    the contributions a Bioconductor developer would make; they should land in a focused repo
    with its own issues and a "how to add a module" guide, not in the ops tracker beside the
    runbooks.
- **Fork PRs never see secrets.** Tests run on `pull_request` against fixtures; deploy runs only
  on push to `main`.
- **Hostname:** `bioc-mcp.seandavi.workers.dev` for v0. A `bioconductor.org` subdomain waits
  on [#39](https://github.com/seandavi/bioc-infrastructure/issues/39).

## Gaps it will expose {#gaps}

These are known before building. Each is a candidate issue on the owning repo, filed once the
adapter shows the cost.

1. **No per-package registry JSON.** The only JSON for one package is an entry in an 8 MB
   `index.json` (2,894 packages). The adapter caches and slices it, but a
   `GET /api/v1/pkg/{universe}/{package}` (index entry + latest observation) would make the
   adapter trivial and the registry API usable by anyone else. **bioc-registry.**
2. **Health is not published.** `bioc-health` produces exactly the ops answers this server
   should give, but only to a shell on onclappc02. **This repo:** run `collect.py` on a timer,
   upload `bundle.json` (findings only; the `config` block and journal tails need review for
   anything not already public) to R2, and add an `ops_health` tool. That is v1.
3. **No "what changed since the last pass".** The registry's parquet holds the history, but
   only DuckDB can reach it. A precomputed `last_pass` / `first_fail` per package and config,
   written by the registry at observation time, would answer the most common triage question
   without SQL. **bioc-registry.**
4. **Stats lag is implicit.** `.tab` files carry no as-of date; the HTML page does.
   **bioc-traffic:** publish `DATA_AS_OF` as a file.

## Acceptance (v0)

- All eight tools return the provenance block, and each has a fixture test.
- `/mcp`, `/mcp/docs` and `/mcp/ops` each list exactly their modules' tools.
- The 30-question docs set: recall@5 measured and reported in the PR.
- Works from Claude Code, Claude Desktop and one non-Anthropic client (Codex or Gemini CLI),
  over the remote URL with no install.
- `bioc://about` lists every upstream and its freshness.
- Nothing returned that is not already reachable at a public URL.

## Next {#next}

- **v1:** gap 2 (`ops_health`, `ops_failing_since`), and gap 1 once the registry route exists.
- **v2:** a `maint` module (`maint_my_packages`, `maint_reverse_deps` with their build state,
  `maint_release_checklist`) over the same adapters, and an `impact` module over the
  bioc-intelligence marts. Same server.
- **Operator, auth-gated:** only if a real question needs non-public data. So far none does.

## Open questions

- Index the `Bioconductor/bioconductor.org` and BiocContributions docs too, or keep the corpus
  to the stack this site describes?
- Does #67's MCP section get rewritten to this trust-based split, or does this page supersede it?
- ADR 0014: add the exception rule ("a community-facing consumer that depends only on public
  URLs keeps its own repo and tracker") to the ADR itself, or record it only here?
